subject: How to fit Gaussian Process with High-Dimensional Data Sets in R-INLA?

messages.author: 39971e2c19b8ec70
messages.subject: How to fit Gaussian Process with High-Dimensional Data Sets in R-INLA?
parts:
Hi guys!

I am new to R-INLA and it really looks like a cool and versatile framework. 
I wonder if I could use INLA to fit high dimensional Gaussian Process (with 8-20 covariates),
i.e.: f(x) ~ GP(m(x), k(x,x',theta)), which is basically a multi-variate normal
distribution with k(x,x',theta) is a squared exponential covariance function, 
basically a function of euclidean distance between two data records (in the high-dimensional 
covariate space).

I was searching through the available models - names(inla.models()$latent) - but I only found 
SPDE models, i.e. spatial, or spatio-temporal, which thus use only two dimensions (maybe three
including time). I need general N-dimensional one.

So I was researching, how could I maybe implement this into R-INLA myself, hopefully in such a way that
I don't need to understand the internals of the Laplace Approximation, just by defining likelihood and kernel functions. 
I found "rgeneric" latent model which allows user to define his own model; but this requires to define function Q 
which returns the precision matrix, which effectively means that I would have to directly invert the covariance 
matrix. That's too heavy computation burden, which isn't necessary (see GRaF R package or 
Rasmussen & Williams 2006: Gaussian processes for machine learning).

So, my question is, how to run these models in R-INLA in most straightforward and simple way?

Thanks a lot!

Tomas

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] How to fit Gaussian Process with High-Dimensional Data Sets in R-INLA?
parts:
There are several issues.
The gain due to sparsity diminished with both dimension and operator order. The exp(-x^2) covariance, aka squared exponential, corresponds to the limiting case of infinite operator order in the Matérn family, so all benefits are lost. However, in practice, squared.exp. fields are virtually indistinguishable from spades with operator 4 and above. And since the squared.exp. covariance is usually a completely arbitrary choice anyway, you could simply change to such a finite order Matérn model instead.

Inla is geared towards such low order Markov property models, which are very efficient when computations are based on the resulting sparse precision matrices, which keep being sparse when conditioning on data, if the nodes of the model have local direct effect (as they do in the spde/GMRF construction we use). This includes the Cholesky factor. The actual inverse (I.e. the covariance matrix) is not needed, so no full inverse is computed. Any model you can come up with that gives you a sparse precision can take advantage of that.

That leaves the dimension issue, for which there is no universal solution. Regularly gridded data could use a kronecker construction, but there is no built in way to take advantage of that for the posterior precision, which will not have a kronecker structure.

If you really do want very smooth field of the type generated by squared exponential covariances, your best bet is probably to define an rgeneric model based on a finite spectral decomposition. That would give a diagonal prior precision matrix, so no need to invert a covariance matrix in the model definition. The posterior would still have a dense precision, but the dimension of the model could be much smaller than the number of data points.

Finn
